body.text: Brazilian voters have denied Latin America’s resurgent right its ultimate prize, snapping a streak of seven straight conservative presidential victories in 18 months.

The stunning triumph of leftist incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva over Flavio Bolsonaro on October 25, with 51.8 per cent of the vote to 48.2 per cent, limits US President Donald Trump’s drive to tighten his grip on the Western Hemisphere and cements Latin America’s most populous country and largest economy as a counterweight to Washington. A Bolsonaro victory would have left Mexico’s Claudia Sheinbaum as the only progressive President among the region’s powerhouses.

For the Trump administration, which has wielded punishing tariffs, severe sanctions and military force to reassert its dominance in the region, Lula’s victory complicates its campaign to enlist Brazil in its military coalition against cartels and to gain preferential access to the country’s critical minerals, analysts say.

Yet both sides see reasons to cooperate. Washington wants access to Brazil’s vast trove of rare earths to reduce its defence industry’s reliance on China. Lula wants foreign investment and tariff relief for Brazilian exporters.

“Lula is pragmatic enough to work out some kind of modus operandi with the Trump administration,” said Will Freeman, a fellow for Latin America studies at the Council on Foreign Relations, adding that the Bolsonaros’ allies in Washington would likely lose sway after the family’s second electoral defeat. Flavio’s father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, lost to Lula in 2022.
“I’m not sure anyone in the Trump administration, beyond a few individuals, will want to keep making the Bolsonaros the central issue in the US-Brazil relationship,” he said.
Flavio Bolsonaro refuses to recognise Lula’s win

Brazilian right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has followed his imprisoned father’s lead by refusing to concede defeat to Lula, who won a historic fourth term in Sunday’s presidential election. Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, called into question a late-Sunday decision by a Lula-appointed Supreme Court justice that extended voting by two hours over alleged voter transport irregularities. He said he would ask for the result to be annulled.

“It is impossible to recognise the election results, given the circumstances under which things unfolded,” Bolsonaro told journalists. Yet the scale of the loss, with Bolsonaro trailing Lula by over 4 million votes, makes it unlikely his efforts to annul the vote will succeed, analysts said. His petition is also undermined by the fact that his campaign also sought a voting extension due to heavy rains in the conservative-leaning south.

Still, Bolsonaro’s refusal to concede could spark a wave of protests in a country where faith in the electoral system, and in judicial independence, has been strained in recent years, observers say. Jair Bolsonaro plunged Brazil into a deep democratic crisis after the election in 2022, when his supporters stormed government buildings in protest against the result. He later received a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup.
Trump’s missing piece

Across much of Latin America, voters fed up with organised crime and economic insecurity have rewarded presidential candidates promising to restore order. From Peru’s Keiko Fujimori to Colombia’s Abelardo de la Espriella and Chile’s José Antonio Kast, newly elected conservatives have courted Trump while taking their cues from El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele, whose sweeping gang crackdown has sharply reduced homicides at the cost of mass arrests and suspended civil liberties.

Trump has reinforced that shift with electoral endorsements, financial bailouts and millions of dollars in military aid. “The US is certainly putting its finger on the scale to try to help the more hard-line right-wing elements in the region,” said Kenneth Roberts, a professor of government at Cornell University.

Brazil would have been Washington’s most consequential addition. Bolsonaro had promised to join the US-led security coalition “with great enthusiasm and great honour”, making his alliance with Trump part of his pitch to voters.

Lula, by contrast, has championed Brazil’s long tradition of nonalignment, cultivating ties with competing powers. His government deepened trade ties with China and sought greater global influence through BRICS, a group of emerging economies.

Trump’s heavy-handed support for the Bolsonaros played into that message. The double-digit tariffs he imposed on a range of Brazilian goods to punish Brazil for prosecuting former President Jair Bolsonaro over a coup plot to oust Lula stirred a nationalist backlash that the leftist leader channelled into the rallying cry “Brazil belongs to Brazilians”.
Wishes pour in

Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who is the current chair of the BRICS geopolitical and economic bloc, which includes Brazil, offered Lula his “heartiest congratulations”. “I look forward to working closely with him to further deepen and expand the multifaceted India-Brazil Strategic Partnership,” Modi added.

Leftist leaders from across the Americas congratulated President Lula. Mexico’s leftist President Claudia Sheinbaum celebrated Lula’s win in a post on X, saying: “Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won.” Cuban President Miguel Diaz-Canel congratulated Lula on his “historic victory that guarantees the continuity of the path of peace, sovereignty, and social justice.”

Argentina’s former President Cristina Kirchner, who is currently under house arrest for corruption, said on X that Lula “knew how to awaken in his compatriots the feeling and sense needed to win”. Uruguay’s President Yamandu Orsi said on X that he had spoken with Lula and “congratulated him on his victory and on the democratic celebration that an electoral process represents”.
EU chief Ursula von der Leyen hailed Lula’s victory as a win for “democracy and multilateralism”.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez celebrated his leftist Brazilian ally Lula da Silva’s re-election victory as launching a “progressive comeback”, as he trails in polls before Spain’s November vote. “A great victory for Lula! What has happened in Brazil will happen in Spain. The global progressive comeback has just begun,” Sanchez posted on X.

French President Emmanuel Macron posted on X: “France and Brazil have much to build together. In the face of the great challenges of our time, let us strengthen our strategic partnership and bring to life the friendship between our two countries in service of a more just world.”

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said at a regular briefing: “China has noted that Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court has announced President Lula has won the second round of the Brazilian general election, and expresses its congratulations.” He added that Beijing was “willing to work with Brazil to continue advancing the building of a China-Brazil community with a shared future”. Asked about Bolsonaro saying he would request an annulment of the elections, Guo said China respects the choice of the Brazilian people.
(With inputs from agencies)
